prize_parts.citation: for the invention and first realisation of spherical-aberration correctors that brought routine sub-angstrom resolution to electron microscopy

statement.case_for: Aberration correction is an invention in the sense of the statutes. Scherzer's 1936 theorem set a limit on rotationally symmetric electron lenses for more than half a century, and the hexapole corrector designed by Rose, built by Haider and shown to work by Urban's group in a corrected TEM broke it. The result is verified by thousands of instruments in independent laboratories, so we do not depend on a single group's claim. It opened a door to what could not be seen before: atom-by-atom imaging and spectroscopy of interfaces, defects, catalysts, 2D materials and quantum devices. Several of the other candidates on this shortlist, the moire materials among them, have been characterised with such instruments. The chain of who did what first is also fairly traceable for a trio: optical design, construction, first demonstration. The topic is mature, and I would say recognition is overdue.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and breadth of support. Krivanek, Dellby and Batson realised a corrector for the scanning (STEM) instrument at nearly the same time, so the three credited names risk crediting only the TEM branch and leaving a visible gap. Only two members ranked this candidate, and one of them (me) ranked it first. I am also aware that a prize for instrumentation can look like a reward for engineering rather than for a discovery about nature. I answer that the Physics Prize has honoured enabling instruments before (the electron microscope itself in 1986), but that answer only holds if the invention is clearly original and the credited people are clearly the originators, and the Krivanek question has to be settled before I would insist on this configuration. My own field makes me a biased judge of how large the impact is.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked aberration correction sixth but called it a true invention with lasting impact on atomic-scale imaging and spectroscopy of materials and interfaces, and named Krivanek, Dellby and Batson as a competing claim that could be contested.
responses.response: I agree with Olle that the credit question is the weak point, and I thank him for raising it plainly. The two lines of work are not the same invention. Rose's hexapole design, Haider's TEM corrector and Urban's demonstration concern the image-forming TEM with Rose's theory behind it. Krivanek's quadrupole-octupole corrector concerns the probe-forming STEM. If the committee thinks the STEM claim is equally original, the options are a three-person prize with a citation that is explicit about the TEM realisation, or a different split of names. I do not want to decide this by prestige. I would ask for the experts to give the dates of the first working corrected TEM and the first corrected STEM, and I remain open to changing the names. I note that Olle's own opening support for a three-name trio is on Rose, Urban and Haider as well.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first: a magic-wavelength proposal that became the most precise measurement devices ever built, near 1e-18, opening relativistic geodesy, constant tests and a redefinition of the second, with Katori and Ye as a clean two-name credit.
responses.response: I take this seriously, and it is my fourth choice and my first alternative. Clocks are the kind of invention that opens a door, and the performance is verified by clock comparisons across continents, which is what I ask of an experimental prize. My reservations are narrower than Stefan's enthusiasm assumes. First, Ye already shares the 2005 prize for the frequency comb that his clock comparisons rely on, so the committee must be clear that this is a separate discovery and not a second prize for the same measurement chain. Second, Stefan himself says Lemonde, Ludlow and others are secondary, and Pearce mentions Takamoto; I would like the experts to say who first demonstrated the Sr lattice clock at the level that proved the idea, because the original experiment, not the most precise one, is the criterion I apply. If that holds, I could move this to first place.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked twisted bilayer graphene fifth and called it still young: the pairing mechanism is not settled, so recognition may be early, and dispute remains about the experimental allocation (Dean, Kim, Yazdani and others).
responses.response: I partly agree with Bernhard on maturity, though I weigh it differently. The prize is for the discovery, and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in the twisted bilayer has been reproduced in many laboratories within a few years, so the experimental result is firm even if the pairing mechanism is not. That is why I rank it second. I do agree with his point about attribution on the experimental side. The 2018 papers had Cao as lead author, and Dean, Kim and Yazdani worked on related moire systems. A three-name configuration would have to leave out Cao, and I do not think that is easy to defend as the original experiment. If the committee wants to move on this candidate, I would like it to say exactly what the citation covers: the prediction plus the first observation, not the whole moire field.

responses.point: Lindroth put clocks first and moire graphene second, with a clean theory-plus-experiment pairing for the latter, and noted Zoller, Bloch and Greiner among her top three ultracold-atom names.
responses.response: I share Eva Lindroth's top two on substance but not the order. Her two-person clock credit and her three-person moire credit are both coherent. I differ in that I give more weight to a tool that changed what a whole community can observe, which I find in aberration correction, over a tool that changed one measurement. I also disagree gently with the idea that quantitative agreement between theory and experiment is the same as a discovery. The aberration corrector is not theory-dependent in this way; it gives a direct image. If the committee prefers the atomic-physics candidates, I would be content to see clocks go forward and would not block it.

uncertainties: Whether the TEM (Rose, Haider, Urban) and STEM (Krivanek, Dellby, Batson) corrector claims are one invention or two, and whether three names can fairly cover both.
Whether the committee will accept an instrument-centred prize when only two of eight members ranked it, and whether it ranks above clocks and moire materials.
Whether Ye's 2005 comb prize reduces the case for Katori and Ye on optical lattice clocks.
How much of the twisted bilayer discovery should be credited to Cao and other experimentalists not named on the shortlist.
statement.conflict_note: I am an electron microscopist and the current President of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so I work in the field of candidate B008 and know its community. My profile does not document a personal or institutional tie to Rose, Urban, Haider or Krivanek, but I may have collaborated with or met some of them through the microscopy societies, and I would accept a recusal discussion on B008 if colleagues think it appropriate. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, which is not related to any shortlisted candidate. No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
